stages.title: Historical research methods
stages.hook: Two historians read the same archive and write opposite conclusions. What in their method could explain the difference, and how would you judge between them?
explain: Historical research begins with a question, not a pile of documents. A good question is answerable with available evidence and situated in a debate. The historian then identifies sources: primary materials (state papers, letters, court records, material objects, oral testimony) and secondary literature (the existing scholarship). Archives are not neutral: what was kept, catalogued or destroyed reflects power, so absences must be interpreted too.

Source criticism has two stages. External criticism asks whether a source is authentic and what its provenance is. Internal criticism asks what the author could know, why it was written and for whom, and how its genre shapes it. Corroboration among independent sources raises confidence, but agreement between sources that copy one another is not independent.

Methods vary. Quantitative history uses serial data such as censuses, tax rolls and ship records. Qualitative approaches read texts closely. Oral history uses interviews, with attention to memory, consent and the community's authority. Digital tools allow text mining of large corpora but do not replace interpretation. Ethical research also considers privacy, consent, repatriation and the voices excluded from the record.

example.q: Two sources describe the same battle and agree closely. Why might that not be strong corroboration?
steps: Check whether they are independent: did one author copy from the other?
Trace each to its origin: if both rely on one lost report, they count as a single witness.
Seek a genuinely independent source, such as an opponent's account or physical evidence.
example.a: Agreement is weak unless the sources are independent of each other.

analogies.sport: A referee's decision is checked against several camera angles, not one repeated view.
analogies.tech: Version history shows how a document changed, as provenance shows a source's chain of custody.
analogies.nature: Ecologists sample many sites rather than one to avoid generalising from an unusual patch.

terms: The documented origin and custody history of a source.
Testing a source's authenticity and date.
Assessing the content's credibility, purpose and perspective.
The absence of certain voices or events in the record.

misc.wrong: History is a matter of collecting facts until the truth emerges.
misc.right: Historians construct arguments from selected evidence, and their questions and methods shape what they find.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: debates continue over how far historical knowledge can be objective, and over the proper balance of quantitative and interpretive methods.

trip.prompt: Identify the stages of source criticism and apply them to a document of your choice.

questions.q: What does external criticism of a source assess?
o: Authenticity and provenance
The emotional tone of the writing and its style
The number of pages the source runs to
The quality of any translation, and nothing more
questions.why: It tests whether the source is genuine and what its origin is.

questions.q: What is archival silence?
o: Absence of certain voices in the record
A quiet reading room inside an archive
Missing page numbers in a bound volume of records
A rule against speaking in the archive
questions.why: What archives omit reflects power and survival, and must be interpreted.

questions.q: Which is a secondary source on the Meiji Restoration?
o: A 2015 scholarly monograph
An 1868 imperial edict
A diary of a samurai from 1868
A photograph from 1870
questions.why: Secondary sources interpret primary evidence later.

questions.q: A historian notices that three chronicles repeat the same details. What is the best next step?
o: Check whether they derive from one source
Count them as three independent witnesses
Discard them
Assume they are true

questions.q: Why is a research question needed before gathering sources?
o: It focuses selection and allows an argument
It guarantees that the answer will be found
It removes all of the researcher's bias
It takes the place of evidence
questions.why: Questions guide what counts as relevant evidence.

questions.q: A community requests control over how its oral histories are used. Which principle is involved?
o: Informed consent and community authority
Expiry of copyright after a fixed period of years
The neutrality of the archive in all matters
Deletion of the data once research is done
questions.why: Ethical oral history respects consent and community rights.

questions.q: What limits the use of text mining on historical corpora?
o: It cannot replace critical interpretation and depends on what has been digitised
It is always accurate whatever the texts
It covers every language equally well
It removes the bias found in the sources
questions.why: Digital corpora are selective and require interpretation.

questions.q: Tax records show a village's grain output rising. Which question best tests whether this means prosperity?
o: Who collected and recorded the data, and how might they have changed it?
What colour and texture is the paper?
How many pages does the document run to?
In which archive is the document now kept?
questions.why: The production of data affects its meaning.

questions.q: Order the stages of a source-based inquiry.
questions.why: Inquiry moves from question to sources, criticism, corroboration and argument.

questions.q: Explain why archives cannot be treated as neutral repositories of the past.
questions.model: Archives preserve what those with power chose to record and keep, so some groups and events are absent or distorted. Historians must interpret both what is present and what is missing.
questions.why: Survival and selection reflect social power.

panel.q: A historian relies only on colonial administrators' reports to describe a rebellion. Evaluate this method.
panel.model: Official reports reflect administrators' aims and views, so relying on them alone risks a one-sided account. The historian should compare them with rebel, local and oral sources and cross-check claims.

panel.q: What does it mean to say a source is evidence of mentalities rather than events?
o: It reveals beliefs and attitudes even if details are inaccurate
It is always false from start to finish
It records the exact facts of what happened
It is a forgery made at a later date
panel.why: Biased or inaccurate sources may still show how people thought.

panel.q: Why does repatriation of human remains and artefacts affect research practice?
o: Ethics and community rights now shape what may be studied and displayed
It brings an end to all research
It has no effect on research practice
It only affects the budgets of museums

teach.model: Historians start with a question, find primary and secondary sources, and test each source's origin and purpose. They check claims against independent sources and build an argument. Archives are shaped by power, so absences matter, and ethics guide work with people's memories and remains.

points.ask: How do you judge a source?
How do you check and what are the limits?

stages.title: Archaeology and material evidence
stages.hook: A burnt seed from a hearth tells us it is 11,460 years old. How can a scientist know that, and how much faith should we place in the number?
explain: Archaeology reconstructs the past from material remains. Context is crucial: the position of an object in the stratigraphy (layers of deposit) shows relative age, since in an undisturbed sequence lower layers are older. Absolute dates come from methods such as radiocarbon dating, which measures the decay of carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years) in organic material, and dendrochronology, which matches tree-ring patterns. Radiocarbon results are calibrated against known records because atmospheric carbon-14 has varied, and dates are reported with uncertainty ranges.

New tools extend evidence. Ancient DNA and isotope analysis reveal ancestry, diet and mobility. Remote sensing such as LiDAR can reveal landscapes beneath forest; a survey in Guatemala published in 2018 revealed tens of thousands of previously unmapped Maya structures. Experimental archaeology tests how things were made and used.

Preservation is uneven: stone and ceramic survive, while textiles, wood and food often do not, and some regions preserve far better than others. Interpretation must avoid equating what survives with what mattered. Ethical questions include who owns the past: the debates over the Benin Bronzes, the Parthenon sculptures and human remains involve colonial acquisition and the rights of source communities.

example.q: A sample has 25% of its original carbon-14. About how old is it, given a half-life of 5,730 years?
steps: After one half-life, 50% remains; after two, 25% remains.
Two half-lives = 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years.
Report with uncertainty and calibration, since the simple model is an approximation.

analogies.nature: Tree rings record wet and dry years like a diary written in wood.
analogies.tech: Calibration is like correcting a clock whose speed varied.
analogies.city: City layers, like a road dug up, expose older pipes under newer ones.

stages.mnemonic: Context, date, test, ask whose past.
terms: The study of layered deposits, in which lower layers are normally older.
The time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.
The study of how remains are preserved or destroyed after deposition.

misc.wrong: Radiocarbon dating can date anything old, including rocks.
misc.right: It applies only to organic material up to roughly 50,000 years old, and its results need calibration.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: dating has error ranges, contamination can mislead, and interpretations of function or belief from objects are inferential.

trip.prompt: Find how calibration curves are built and why raw dates differ from calendar years.

questions.q: A wooden tool has 25% of its original carbon-14. Using a half-life of 5,730 years, how old is it, in years (uncalibrated)?
What percentage of the original carbon-14 remains after three half-lives?
In undisturbed stratigraphy, which layer is generally oldest?
o: The lowest
The highest
The thickest
The darkest
questions.why: Layers are deposited in sequence, from bottom to top.

questions.q: What does dendrochronology measure?
o: Tree-ring patterns
Magnetic patterns in rocks
Pollen grains in soil layers
The density of ancient bone
questions.why: Ring widths match across trees to give calendar dates.

questions.q: Why are radiocarbon dates calibrated?
o: Atmospheric carbon-14 levels varied over time
Samples change colour as they grow older
Labs around the world use different units
The half-life of carbon-14 has changed over time

questions.q: Which can radiocarbon dating be used on?
o: Charcoal from a hearth
A granite wall of a temple
A bronze sword from a grave
The clay of a fired pot

questions.q: A site yields many pots but no cloth. What should the archaeologist consider?
o: Preservation bias: textiles rarely survive
That the people there had no cloth at all, ever
That cloth was banned in that society
That only the pots were of any importance
questions.why: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

questions.q: What did the 2018 LiDAR survey in Guatemala show?
o: Tens of thousands of unmapped Maya structures beneath forest
That no Maya cities lay under the forest
A single temple standing alone
A network of Inca roads in the jungle
questions.why: It revised estimates of Maya population and landscape modification.

questions.q: Order the steps in dating a hearth sample.
items: Calibrate the result and give an error range
questions.why: Context and careful sampling precede measurement and calibration.

questions.q: Why should historians be cautious about inferring a society's beliefs from objects alone?
questions.model: Objects do not state their meaning, so function and belief are inferred and can be ambiguous; interpretation needs context, written sources where they exist, and awareness that only some objects survive.

panel.q: Why is looting more damaging than the loss of a single object?
o: It destroys context that gives objects meaning
It lowers the prices of antiquities on the market
It improves research by moving objects around
It does not matter once an object is sold

panel.q: What is a strongest argument for returning contested artefacts?
o: They were acquired under colonial power imbalances and matter to source communities
They are cheaper to look after at home
Museums are unable to protect them
Nobody in the world wants them
panel.why: Restitution debates centre on legitimacy and heritage rights; counterarguments about access and stewardship also exist.

panel.q: Why combine ancient DNA with archaeology?
o: Genetic and material evidence together can show ancestry and cultural change
DNA is able to replace archaeology completely
DNA evidence is perfect and never wrong
Archaeology has been shown to be invalid
panel.why: Genes and culture do not always match, so both are needed.

teach.model: Archaeologists recover objects and record the layers they come from, because context shows relative age. Radiocarbon dating measures decay of carbon-14 in organic material and is calibrated, while tree rings give calendar dates. Preservation is uneven and interpretation is inferential, and ethics shape the work.

stages.title: Historiography and competing interpretations
stages.hook: Historians have called the same event a revolution, a coup and a civil war. What does this tell us about writing history?
explain: Historiography is the study of how history has been written. The 19th-century Rankean tradition emphasised archival documents and states. Marxist historians stressed class and economic structures. The French Annales school, with Fernand Braudel, looked at long-term structures (the longue durée), geography and everyday life. Social history, women's history, microhistory and cultural history widened the subject.

Postcolonial approaches challenge Eurocentric narratives. Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) argued that Western scholarship often constructed 'the Orient' as an exotic Other. The Subaltern Studies group in South Asia sought to write the history of those excluded from elite narratives. Global history traces connections and comparisons across regions rather than telling history nation by nation.

Interpretations compete on concrete questions: the origins of the First World War, the causes of the Industrial Revolution, the Great Divergence between Europe and Asia (Kenneth Pomeranz argued that coal and colonial resources mattered), the role of ideas versus economics in revolutions. Competing interpretations are not simply opinions: they are judged by evidence, logic, and how well they explain.

example.q: Why do historians disagree about the Great Divergence?
steps: They weigh different causes: institutions, coal, colonial trade, culture.
They use different data and comparisons, such as the Yangtze delta versus England.
Because the data are partial, several explanations can fit, so argument continues.
example.a: Different causal weights, data and comparisons.

analogies.sport: Commentators analyse the same match differently, but the video evidence limits what can be claimed.
analogies.music: Different performers interpret the same score; the score constrains the range.
analogies.tech: Scientists argue over models fitted to the same data.

stages.mnemonic: School, lens, evidence: each school is a lens, and evidence tests it.
terms: The study of how history is written and interpreted.
Braudel's term for long-term historical structures.
A person or group excluded from power; used in Subaltern Studies.
Interpreting the world mainly through European experience.

misc.wrong: If historians disagree, all interpretations are equally valid.
misc.right: Interpretations differ in how well they use evidence and explain it; some are better supported than others.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: even the labels of schools are contested, and many historians combine approaches.

trip.prompt: Choose two schools and compare how each would study the same event.

questions.q: What is historiography?
o: The study of how history is written
A type of map used by historians and archivists
A method for dating old documents
A legal system used in archives
questions.why: It examines historians' methods and interpretations.

questions.q: Who emphasised the longue durée?
o: Fernand Braudel
Leopold von Ranke
Edward Said
Kenneth Pomeranz

questions.q: What did Said's Orientalism (1978) argue?
o: Western scholarship often constructed an exotic 'Orient' as Other
Eastern scholars invented the study of history
Trade was the main driver of empire
Scholarly writing is always neutral
questions.why: It critiqued representations that supported colonial power.

questions.q: What is the aim of Subaltern Studies?
o: Writing history from the perspective of those excluded by elites
Studying only the history of rulers
Studying the history of underground railways
Mapping the borders of states

questions.q: What does 'Eurocentrism' mean?
o: Interpreting the world mainly through European experience
Studying Europe and nothing else
The study of the Euro currency
A style of drawing maps only
questions.why: It treats Europe as the norm.

questions.q: Two historians weigh different causes for the Industrial Revolution. What explains this?
o: They use different evidence, comparisons and causal weights
One of them must be lying
History can never truly be known
Their dates for events differ
questions.why: Interpretation involves judgement over partial evidence.

questions.q: Which is the best response to disagreement between interpretations?
o: Assess evidence, logic and explanatory power
Choose the one that you like best
Declare all of them equally good
Ignore both of them completely

questions.q: Why does global history complement national history?
o: It traces connections and comparisons across regions
It ignores nations altogether
It covers only trade and nothing else
It rejects the use of evidence

questions.q: Match the approach to its emphasis.
Explain why competing historical interpretations are not merely matters of opinion.
questions.model: Interpretations are argued from evidence and reasoning and can be judged on how well they account for the sources and withstand scrutiny, so some are better supported than others.

panel.q: Critically assess the claim that national histories are the natural unit of historical study.
panel.model: National units can be anachronistic and obscure cross-border networks such as trade and migration; they are useful but are constructed frames, so global and comparative approaches complement them.

panel.q: Why was 'Eurocentric' history problematic?
o: It treated Europe's path as universal and sidelined other regions' agency
It was too accurate about the world
It was too global in scope
It left Europe out of the story

panel.q: What risk arises in reacting against Eurocentrism?
o: Reversing into another centrism instead of balanced, evidence-based comparison
Gaining accuracy automatically
Ending all debate between scholars
Removing the need for sources
panel.why: The aim is balance, not replacement.

teach.model: Historiography studies how history is written. Schools such as the Rankean, Marxist and Annales approaches ask different questions, and postcolonial and global history challenge Eurocentric narratives. Interpretations compete but are judged by evidence and reasoning, not opinion.

stages.title: Comparative history of world civilisations
stages.hook: Rome and Han China were each ruling tens of millions of people at about the same time, with no knowledge of each other beyond rumour. What can comparing them reveal?
explain: Comparative history asks why similar problems produced different or similar solutions. Han China (206 BCE to 220 CE) and the Roman Empire (at its peak in the 2nd century CE) each governed populations estimated in the tens of millions, built roads and fortifications, collected taxes, and faced pressure on their frontiers. Differences include Rome's reliance on provincial elites and legions and the Han's civil-service ideology drawing on Confucianism. Both had slavery or forced labour in different forms, and both fragmented politically, yet China was repeatedly reunified.

Comparison requires care. Similarities do not imply contact or a universal pattern. Karl Jaspers' idea of an 'Axial Age' (roughly 800 to 200 BCE), when philosophies emerged in China, India, Persia, Israel and Greece, is influential but contested because it groups very different traditions. Collapse is another theme: around 1200 BCE the Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean societies broke down, and scholars debate the combined roles of climate, migration, warfare and trade disruption.

A good comparison states its criteria, treats cases as equals, and does not rank civilisations on a single scale. Questions might be about state capacity, agricultural productivity, trade networks, religion and law.

example.q: Why is it misleading to ask 'which civilisation was greater'?
steps: 'Greater' needs a criterion: size, durability, art, welfare, science.
Different criteria give different rankings, so the ranking depends on the chooser.
A better question compares how each handled a specific problem.
example.a: The ranking depends on arbitrary criteria; compare specific problems instead.

analogies.farm: Two farms in different climates grow different crops well; neither is better in general.
analogies.music: Different instruments are suited to different pieces; they are not ranked.
analogies.sea: Two ports can be compared by cargo, depth and trade, but each serves a different coast.

terms: The systematic comparison of cases to explain similarities and differences.
Jaspers' term for an era of widespread philosophical and religious innovation.
A state's ability to tax, administer and enforce.
A major loss of political and economic complexity.

misc.wrong: Civilisations rise and fall in a fixed cycle.
misc.right: Trajectories vary, and 'collapse' often involves transformation and continuity as well as loss.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: population estimates for antiquity are rough, and the Axial Age idea and Bronze Age collapse causes are debated.

trip.prompt: List the proposed causes and the evidence offered for each.

questions.q: What is the purpose of comparative history?
o: To explain similarities and differences between cases
To rank societies from best to worst
To prove that one society was the best
To make a list of dates

questions.q: Roughly when was the Bronze Age collapse?
o: Around 1200 BCE
Around 500 CE
Around 1500 CE
Around 3000 BCE
questions.why: Many eastern Mediterranean societies declined c.1200 BCE.

questions.q: Who proposed the Axial Age?
o: Karl Jaspers
Fernand Braudel
Edward Said
Ibn Khaldun

questions.q: Why is the Axial Age concept contested?
o: It groups very different traditions under one pattern
It gives no dates for the period
It names no places at all
It was proposed only recently

questions.q: A claim states that civilisation X was 'more advanced' than Y. What should a historian ask?
o: Advanced by what criterion, and for what purpose?
Which one was bigger in area?
Which one was older?
Which one had more gold?

questions.q: Which comparison is methodologically sound?
o: Comparing how Rome and Han China taxed and administered provinces
Deciding which empire was morally better
Assuming the two were in contact
Ranking the two by their size alone
questions.why: It uses stated criteria and equal treatment.

questions.q: Why can similarities between societies not be taken to show contact?
o: Similar problems can produce similar solutions independently
They always show that contact took place
They show links of race or descent
They show that one society copied the other

questions.q: Why is 'collapse' a contested term?
o: Some change involves transformation and continuity, not total ending
It has no meaning for historians
It always means that a people vanished
It is simply the name of a date

questions.q: Match the state to its characteristic.
pairs: Civil service ideology drawing on Confucianism
questions.why: Different states used different tools of administration.

questions.q: Explain why comparing civilisations on a single scale of 'greatness' is flawed.
questions.model: 'Greatness' depends on chosen criteria that are subjective and culturally loaded; different criteria give different rankings, so comparison should address specific questions in context without ranking.

panel.q: Evaluate the claim that environmental stress alone explains the Bronze Age collapse.
panel.model: Evidence for drought exists, but most scholars see the collapse as an interaction of climate, migration, warfare and disrupted trade, so a single cause oversimplifies; the evidence is incomplete and debated.
panel.why: Single-cause explanations rarely fit complex events.

panel.q: What is a risk of comparing only large empires?
o: It overlooks smaller societies, such as stateless peoples with complex institutions
It covers too many societies at once
It is always the correct approach
It lacks any evidence to use

panel.q: What makes a comparison fair?
o: Stated criteria and equal attention to each case's context
Judging every case by one's own values
Ignoring the differences between cases
Leaving out evidence that does not fit

teach.model: Comparative history studies why societies solved similar problems in similar or different ways, such as how Rome and Han China governed large populations. It uses stated criteria, treats cases as equals and avoids ranking. Ideas like the Axial Age and collapse are useful but contested.

stages.title: Global economic history
stages.hook: Silver mined in the Andes in the 1500s ended up in Chinese markets. How did a single metal link economies across the world, and what does this say about when the world became 'global'?
explain: Global economic history traces long-distance exchange, production and inequality. Trade networks such as the Silk Road and the Indian Ocean existed for centuries before 1500. After about 1550, silver from Potosí (in today's Bolivia) and Mexico flowed to Europe and, via Manila galleons from 1565, to China, where silver was in demand for taxes and trade. Enslaved Africans' labour on Atlantic plantations produced sugar and cotton for world markets. These links make the early modern era a major step in global integration, though 'globalisation' is debated for earlier periods.

The Great Divergence names the widening gap in income between parts of Western Europe and China and India from the 1700s and 1800s. Explanations include coal and access to colonial resources (Pomeranz), institutions, culture, and demography. Historians such as Eric Williams argued that Atlantic slavery contributed to British industrialisation; the size of its role remains debated.

Economic historians use data such as wages, prices and national accounts, including reconstructions by Angus Maddison. Growth is often described with compound rates: at a steady growth of g per year, output doubles in about 70 ÷ g years (a rule of thumb), so 2% growth doubles output in roughly 35 years.

example.q: At a constant 2% annual growth, about how many years until an economy's output doubles? Use ln 2 ÷ ln 1.02.
steps: Doubling means (1.02)^t = 2.
t ≈ 35.0 years; the rule of 70 gives 70 ÷ 2 = 35.

analogies.sea: Silver moved across oceans like a currency of the first global market.
analogies.farm: A plantation economy is like a farm designed to feed distant factories.
analogies.tech: A payments network connects banks; the silver trade connected states.

stages.mnemonic: Silver, sugar, cotton, coal: four goods that tied the world.
terms: The rising income gap between parts of Western Europe and much of Asia from the 1700s-1800s.
A Spanish trade ship across the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco from 1565.
Growth in which each period's increase builds on the previous total.

misc.wrong: Europe was always richer than Asia.
misc.right: Estimates suggest living standards in parts of Asia were comparable with Europe's until around the 1700s; the gap widened later.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: pre-modern income estimates are reconstructions with wide error margins, and the causes of the Great Divergence are debated.

trip.prompt: Compare Pomeranz's argument with an institutional explanation.

A war between rival empires

Angus Maddison, the economic historian

Explain why silver linked the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia in the early modern world.
questions.model: Silver mined in the Americas moved to Europe and, by Atlantic and Pacific routes, to China, where demand was high; it financed trade, including in goods produced by enslaved Africans, linking the four regions.

panel.q: Why does GDP per capita hide important differences?
o: It ignores distribution and non-market work
It gives the exact figure for every single person
It includes everything that people produce
It measures only cultural wealth

panel.q: Why compare Yangtze delta and England in the Great Divergence debate?
o: Both were advanced regions, so differences help test explanations
The two regions were identical

panel.why: Comparison of like regions avoids bias.

panel.q: What caution applies to the phrase 'the rise of the West'?
o: It can obscure Asia's and Africa's roles and the contingency of outcomes
It is neutral and free of any bias
It is exact in all its claims
It covers the whole of history

teach.model: Trade networks linked regions long before 1500. After about 1550, silver from the Americas flowed to Europe and China, and slave labour fed Atlantic plantation trade. The Great Divergence describes the widening income gap from the 1700s and 1800s, with several debated explanations.

stages.title: History of science, engineering and medicine
stages.hook: Long before Edward Jenner's vaccine in 1796, people in China, India, Africa and the Ottoman world were deliberately exposing others to mild smallpox. What does this say about how medical knowledge develops?
explain: Science, engineering and medicine have grown through exchange and local innovation. Smallpox variolation (inoculation with material from a mild case) was practised in several regions before Jenner. Jenner's vaccination in 1796 used cowpox, and a global campaign led to the WHO's declaration in 1980 that smallpox had been eradicated, the only human disease so far eradicated by deliberate effort.

Medicine also changed through evidence. In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera cases in London to a contaminated water pump, supporting a water-borne explanation. Pasteur and Koch's work in the 1860s to 1880s established germ theory, and Fleming noticed the effects of penicillin in 1928. Earlier texts such as Sushruta's Indian surgical writings, Ibn Sina's Canon and Chinese medical classics show long, parallel traditions.

In engineering and mathematics, qanat water tunnels in Persia, Roman concrete, Inca roads and suspension bridges, and Chinese hydraulic engineering solved local problems. Brahmagupta (628 CE) set out rules for zero as a number, and al-Khwarizmi's work helped systematise algebra. Historians of science avoid simple 'firsts' and ask who produced knowledge, how it travelled, and who was credited.

example.q: Why does John Snow's cholera map count as evidence rather than proof?
steps: Cases clustered around one pump, supporting a water-borne cause.
He also checked exceptions, such as a brewery with no cases.
Later microbiology confirmed the bacterium, but the map alone showed an association.
example.a: It showed a strong association that later work confirmed.

analogies.city: A qanat is like an underground aqueduct that avoids evaporation.
analogies.sport: Vaccines train the body like a practice match before the real game.
analogies.tech: Open peer review of germ theory is like testing software in public.

terms: Deliberate inoculation with smallpox material to induce milder disease.
The theory that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
A gently sloping underground channel carrying water.
Permanent reduction of a disease to zero worldwide.

misc.wrong: Scientific progress comes from lone geniuses in one place.
misc.right: It results from networks, translation, craft knowledge and collaboration across cultures.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: priority claims (who was 'first') are often disputed, and dating of ancient texts such as Sushruta's is uncertain.

trip.prompt: Trace variolation, Jenner's vaccine and eradication on one timeline.

questions.q: When did the WHO declare smallpox eradicated?
What did Jenner use for vaccination in 1796?
o: Cowpox material
Material from smallpox scabs
The drug penicillin

questions.q: What did John Snow's 1854 map support?
o: A water-borne cause of cholera
The old theory of bad air as the cause

teach.model: Medical and scientific knowledge grew through networks across many cultures. stages.title: Colonialism, postcolonialism and historical memory
stages.hook: In 2021 Germany formally acknowledged the killings of Herero and Nama peoples in Namibia as genocide. Why do states change how they remember the past, and who decides?
explain: Postcolonial studies examine the legacies of colonialism in politics, economies, knowledge and culture. Frantz Fanon analysed the psychological and political effects of colonial rule and the struggle against it. Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) examined how representations supported domination. The Subaltern Studies group argued for histories from below. Writers such as Aimé Césaire and the Négritude movement reclaimed Black identity and history.

Historical memory is how societies remember and commemorate the past. Memory is selective and political: monuments, holidays, textbooks and museums express what a society chooses to honour. Pierre Nora described 'sites of memory' (lieux de mémoire). Debates over statues, street names and museum collections show contested memory.

Formal processes address past wrongs. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (from 1996) heard testimony on apartheid-era abuses. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2008 to 2015) examined the residential school system for Indigenous children. In 2008 Australia's Prime Minister apologised to the Stolen Generations. Such processes raise questions about truth, justice, reparation and who is included.

example.q: Why can an apology be both significant and insufficient?
steps: It publicly acknowledges harm, which can matter to survivors.
Without changes such as redress or policy, it may seem symbolic.
Different groups may judge differently, so assessment needs their voices.
example.a: It acknowledges harm, but its value depends on action and the views of those affected.

analogies.city: Renaming a street or removing a statue changes what a city says about itself.
analogies.home: A family decides which stories to tell at gatherings, and which to leave unspoken.
analogies.music: A national anthem is a choice of what to commemorate.

terms: Critical study of the legacies of colonialism and of resistance to it.
How groups remember and commemorate the past.
Returning property or making amends for loss.
Processes to rebuild relationships after conflict or injustice.

misc.wrong: Postcolonial history simply blames the past.
misc.right: It analyses structures, representations and legacies using evidence, and it includes agency and resistance.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: scholars debate how to measure colonial legacies and what forms of redress are appropriate; views differ within affected communities.

questions.q: Explain why public memory of colonialism differs between formerly colonised and former colonial societies.
questions.model: Colonised societies often remember dispossession and resistance, while former colonial powers may remember empire selectively through pride or forgetting; each group's experiences and narratives shape what is commemorated, so memory is contested.

panel.q: Evaluate whether truth commissions achieve reconciliation.
panel.model: They can record testimony and acknowledge harm, but trade-offs with justice, limited reparations and unresolved structural inequality mean outcomes are mixed and depend on context and on how survivors judge them.

teach.model: Postcolonial studies examine colonialism's legacies and the ways it was represented and resisted. Societies remember the past selectively through monuments, textbooks and museums, and memory is often contested. Truth commissions, apologies and restitution are attempts to address past harm, with mixed results.

stages.title: Indigenous and oral historical traditions
stages.hook: In 1997 the Supreme Court of Canada ruled in Delgamuukw that oral histories must be given appropriate weight as evidence of Indigenous land claims. Why had courts and historians once been reluctant to accept them?
explain: Oral traditions are bodies of knowledge transmitted by speech, song and ceremony across generations. Jan Vansina's work on oral tradition as history showed that methods exist to evaluate them: examining how they are transmitted, who is authorised to tell them, how they relate to other evidence and what purposes they serve. Written sources can also be biased; the aim is not to rank oral against written but to read each critically.

Examples are diverse: West African griots, Māori whakapapa (genealogies) recited to link people to ancestors and land, and Aboriginal Australian songlines that encode routes and landscapes. Some scholars have proposed that Aboriginal stories preserve memories of events from the end of the last Ice Age, such as rising seas, and that Gunditjmara stories may refer to volcanic activity at Budj Bim; these claims are debated, with some researchers cautioning about dating and interpretation.

Respect and rights matter. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) affirms Indigenous peoples' rights over their cultures and knowledge. Principles such as CARE (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics) guide Indigenous data governance. Collaboration with communities, rather than extraction, is now central to research.

example.q: How might a historian test an oral tradition about a past flood?
steps: Establish who tells it, under what rules, and how it was transmitted.
Compare it with independent evidence, such as geology, archaeology or written sources.
Report agreement and disagreement and acknowledge limits, in collaboration with the community.
example.a: Evaluate transmission, compare with independent evidence, and report limits with the community.

analogies.music: A song carries a story through rhythm and melody that help memory.
analogies.nature: A landscape marked by stories works like a map made of places and meanings.
analogies.home: A family recites ancestors' names at gatherings, keeping genealogy alive.

The right of Indigenous peoples to govern data about their communities.

misc.right: They have their own methods of preservation and can hold valuable evidence, and all sources require critical reading.

stages.limits: Oral tradition: community knowledge is authoritative within its own frameworks. Scholarly uncertainty: whether particular stories preserve specific ancient events is debated and cannot be proven beyond doubt in most cases.

teach.topic: Indigenous and oral traditions as history
teach.model: Oral traditions pass knowledge through speech, song and ceremony, and scholars have methods to evaluate them, such as examining transmission and comparing with independent evidence. They must be treated respectfully and with community consent, and some claims about very ancient memory are debated.

stages.title: Integrated cross-continental historical investigation
stages.hook: Ice drilled from Antarctica holds air bubbles from up to about 800,000 years ago, while silver from the Andes funded trade in Asia. Can we design one investigation that connects such different kinds of evidence across continents?
explain: An integrated investigation begins with a question that spans regions, then selects cases, sources and methods that fit it. Take the question: how did the movement of silver and goods after 1550 connect the Americas, Africa, Europe and Asia, and with what consequences for different peoples? Evidence includes mine records from Potosí, shipping logs of the Manila galleons, Chinese tax and market records, plantation and slave-voyage databases, and accounts by enslaved, Indigenous and mercantile voices. Each region's sources must be read in context, and absence of some voices must be noted.

Different kinds of evidence answer different questions. Proxy evidence, such as ice cores from Antarctica (EPICA Dome C reaches back about 800,000 years), tree rings and lake sediments, can show past climate and pollution, such as evidence of lead and later of industrial emissions. Antarctica has no Indigenous history, so its record is of exploration, science and the natural archive in the ice, a reminder that history includes environmental evidence.

A strong investigation states criteria, compares fairly, avoids ranking civilisations, weighs perspectives, and ends with an argument qualified by uncertainty. It acknowledges what documented fact supports, what scholars debate, and where oral traditions offer their own authority.

example.q: How would you structure an investigation of silver's global links?
steps: Question: how did silver connect regions after 1550, and who gained or lost?
Evidence: mine, shipping and tax records, plantation databases, and accounts from varied perspectives.
Method: compare regions on shared criteria, corroborate across sources, and state limits.
example.a: A question, varied sources from several regions, a fair comparison and an argument with stated limits.

analogies.nature: Ice, rings and sediment are nature's archives, like layers in a book.
analogies.sea: Shipping logs trace routes as a map traces roads.
analogies.tech: A database links records from many places, as an index links books in many libraries.

stages.mnemonic: Question, cases, sources, compare, argue, qualify.
terms: Indirect natural records of past conditions, such as ice cores.
Using several independent kinds of evidence to test a claim.
Choosing which examples to study and why.
The role of chance and choice in how events unfolded.

misc.wrong: Global history means summarising everything everywhere.
misc.right: It uses focused questions and well-chosen cases to trace connections and comparisons rigorously.

stages.limits: Documented fact: archive and ice-core records exist. Scholarly uncertainty: interpreting proxies and economic data involves error ranges; oral traditions are authoritative within their communities and complement other evidence.

questions.q: Explain how documentary and environmental evidence can complement each other in historical research.
questions.model: Documents show human decisions and experiences, while proxies like ice cores and tree rings show environmental conditions; combining and cross-checking them gives a fuller, more reliable picture.
questions.why: Different evidence answers different parts of a question.

panel.q: Design a fair way to compare responses to a pandemic in the 14th century across Eurasia and North Africa. State two principles.
panel.model: Use the same stated questions for each region, draw on local sources in several languages, take account of different records, avoid ranking and state the uneven evidence.

All regions have equal records

Hide the debate from readers
panel.why: Honesty about uncertainty is part of rigour.

teach.model: An integrated investigation starts with a question that spans regions, chooses cases and varied sources, compares them on stated criteria without ranking, and ends with an argument that states its limits. It can combine documents, oral traditions and environmental records like ice cores.
